title: CCI Fines Agro-Input Dealer Associations for Cartel to Boycott Online Platforms
meta_description: CCI penalises two dealer associations and two office bearers for organising a boycott of online agro-input platforms such as AgroStar.
case_name: In Re: Cartelisation by Agro Input Dealers Association and Agro Input Welfare Association
citation: Order dated 21 August 2026 under Section 27 of the Competition Act, 2002
body: Farmers buying seeds, pesticides and fertiliser online are supposed to benefit from more sellers competing for their business. The Competition Commission of India found that two dealer associations tried to make sure that competition never showed up in the first place, by pressuring their own members and the companies that supply them to stay off platforms such as AgroStar.

Information filed by Ulink Agritech Private Limited, which runs the AgroStar app, set the case in motion. Ulink alleged that the Agro Input Dealers Association and the Agro Input Welfare Association had threatened retailers and manufacturers, warning them against selling through online agro-input platforms. The CCI's Director General traced the campaign back to a written communication dated 5 August 2022, in which the Agro Input Dealers Association had called on agri-input companies to stop selling through such platforms altogether.

That call to arms ran directly against a change the law itself had made. Rule 10(E) of the Insecticides Rules, 1971, inserted through a 2022 amendment, permits licensees to sell insecticides through e-commerce entities, subject to the usual regulatory conditions. The associations were, in effect, organising resistance to a channel the Insecticides Rules had already opened up, using their collective weight over retailers and manufacturers to keep that channel closed in practice.

Establishing that conduct took more than pointing to the 2022 communication on its own. The Director General's investigation had to show that the associations' call to boycott actually translated into retailers and manufacturers altering their own commercial behaviour under pressure, rather than through independent business judgment. Information, complaints, threats and a visible pattern of compliance all had to line up before the Commission would treat a trade body's call to its members as an enforceable cartel decision rather than mere advocacy.

On that evidentiary foundation, the Commission held the conduct in contravention of Section 3(3)(b) of the Competition Act, 2002, which covers agreements, including decisions by trade associations, that limit or control production, supply, markets, technical development, investment or the provision of services. A coordinated campaign discouraging an entire category of sellers from using a lawful sales channel is exactly the kind of market-controlling decision that provision targets, regardless of whether the associations called it advocacy or self-regulation among themselves.

By its order of 21 August 2026, passed under Section 27 of the Act, the CCI imposed monetary penalties on the Agro Input Dealers Association, the Agro Input Welfare Association, and two individuals identified as office bearers, Manmohan C. Kalantri and Arvindbhai Jerambhai Patel. Alongside the penalties, the Commission issued a cease and desist direction and required the associations to put their members through competition-compliance training going forward, a remedy aimed as much at changing how these bodies operate as at punishing what they already did.

None of this friction is unique to agro-inputs. Offline dealer networks built up over decades across several Indian sectors have watched manufacturers add direct online channels, and some trade bodies have responded by leaning on collective bargaining power over distribution rather than competing on service or price. Where that response takes the form of coordinated pressure rather than individual retailers simply choosing to stay offline, the Competition Act treats it as a market-sharing decision between competitors acting in concert, dressed up as association policy. An association that lobbies regulators or negotiates collectively on lawful terms stays on safe ground; one that tells members which legitimate sales channels they may not use has crossed into territory Section 3(3)(b) exists to police.

Companies in agriculture, FMCG and any other sector where dealer associations hold real sway over distribution should treat this order as a warning rather than a one-off. Trade bodies that issue circulars discouraging members from dealing with online platforms, or that organise informal boycotts against competitors using new sales channels, are exposed to the same Section 3(3)(b) analysis applied here, and the compliance training this order requires of the associations is a signal that repeat conduct afterward would invite a harsher response the second time around. Manufacturers on the receiving end of similar pressure now have a concrete precedent to point to if they choose to complain to the Commission instead of quietly falling in line.
why_it_matters: Trade and dealer associations that pressure members to boycott lawful online sales channels, rather than simply advocating for members' interests, face penalties under Section 3(3)(b) of the Competition Act. Manufacturers and e-commerce platforms facing such coordinated resistance from offline dealer networks in agriculture or other sectors now have a concrete CCI precedent to rely on when deciding whether to approach the Commission.
card_summary: CCI penalises two agro-input dealer associations and two office bearers for organising a boycott against online platforms like AgroStar, holding the conduct a cartel under Section 3(3)(b).
card_tip: A trade association that pressures members to boycott a lawful sales channel, rather than just lobbying on their behalf, risks Section 3(3)(b) liability regardless of how it describes its own conduct.
verification_notes: The order date (21 August 2026), the statutory basis (Section 27 read with Section 3(3)(b)), the parties penalised (Agro Input Dealers Association, Agro Input Welfare Association, Manmohan C. Kalantri, Arvindbhai Jerambhai Patel), the informant (Ulink Agritech, operator of AgroStar), and the underlying 5 August 2022 communication are confirmed through the CCI's own press release as reproduced in a LiveLawBiz-hosted PDF, and corroborated by independent law firm newsletters (DSK Legal, AMSShardul) and a secondary legal commentary site. The composition of the CCI bench that passed the order was not confirmed in the sources reviewed and is left unstated rather than guessed.
